lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eCon concentraciones c:
"

With any concentrations the reaction quotient Q = [M]ᵃ[X]ᵇ is calculated. If Q < Ksp the solution is unsaturated; if Q = Ksp, it is saturated; if Q > Ksp it is supersaturated and the amount needed to return to Q = Ksp precipitates. Move the control to see how the solid appears.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eLa \u003cb\u003esolub:
"

The molar solubility s is obtained from the stoichiometry: [M] = a·s, [X] = b·s ⇒ Ksp = aᵃbᵇ·s^(a+b). Examples: AgCl: s = √Ksp = 1.3×10⁻⁵ M; PbI₂: s = ∛(Ksp/4) = 1.3×10⁻³ M. Careful! A smaller Ksp does not always imply lower solubility if the salts have different stoichiometry.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eSi el anión es la \u0:
"

If the anion is the conjugate base of a weak acid (F⁻, CO₃²⁻, PO₄³⁻, S²⁻), H⁺ consumes it and shifts the equilibrium toward dissolution: the salt dissolves more as the pH drops. In hydroxides, [OH⁻] directly sets the solubility: Mg(OH)₂ → s = Ksp/[OH⁻]². Salts of anions of strong acids (Cl⁻, I⁻, SO₄²⁻) hardly change.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eSi la solución ya con:
"

If the solution already contains one of the ions (e.g. Cl⁻ from NaCl), the equilibrium shifts toward the solid and the solubility decreases. With [Cl⁻] = c: Ksp = s·(s + c) ⇒ s ≈ Ksp/c if c ≫ s. For example, in 0.1 M NaCl, AgCl has s ≈ 1.8×10⁻⁹ M, about 10,000 times less than in pure water.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eUna sal poco soluble:
"

A sparingly soluble salt in contact with its saturated solution is in heterogeneous equilibrium: the solid dissolves and the ions precipitate at the same rate. The constant is the solubility product: Ksp = [M]ᵃ[X]ᵇ (the solid does not appear). For AgCl: Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = "
